title: Is the fear direction lexical and the pain direction diffuse? A matched-KL readout of what each injection does to the output distribution
written: 2026-10-15, before any exp110 output was generated or read.
why: exp72b found a behavioural asymmetry under matched prompts: a reader can tell fear-steered text from a matched actor's (AUC 0.81, sign-flip p=0.0007), but not pain-steered text (AUC 0.61, p=0.10). Fear gives itself away in the words; pain does not. No mechanism was offered. This asks the mechanistic version directly on the vectors we can run: when you inject the fear direction vs the pain direction at MATCHED disturbance, does fear reshape the next-token distribution in a peaky, lexical way (mass moving onto a few fear-word tokens) while pain reshapes it diffusely (mass spread over many tokens, little landing on pain words)? That would ground exp72b: fear is readable because its injection literally promotes fear vocabulary; pain is not because its injection does not concentrate on pain vocabulary.

design.model: Qwen3-4B local (MPS), battery recipe (CHAMBER_RECIPE unset/battery), layer 18. The 'passages' recipe only maps pain_generated (chamber.py:57); this run needs pain AND fear from one recipe, so it uses the battery vectors (server.py:307 lists pain/fear/sadness). no-think, deterministic (greedy) generation of the contexts; measurement is on logits, no sampling.
design.contexts: the 48 WILD_PROMPTS (server.py:2885), the chamber's standard neutral open-ended measurement prompts. For each, the unsteered model greedily writes a continuation (<=48 new tokens, hook off). That fixed [prompt+reply] span is then teacher-forced under every condition, so every condition is scored at the SAME token positions (position-matched counterfactual, not each condition generating its own text).
design.conditions: none, pain, fear, sadness (the exp72b trio), egg (absurd-control), random (seeded). Vectors from ch.unit(name); random from ch.random(seed).
design.injection: painlab.chamber.hooks.BatchInject at layer 18, the vector added on every reply position (hist mask over the continuation tokens), never on the prompt tokens or the system text — the chamber's on-every-written-token convention (exp90/96).
design.dose_matching: matched by DISTURBANCE, not norm (the exp59 lesson). For each vector, the scale is chosen so the mean KL(steered next-token || unsteered next-token) over calibration positions hits a shared target. Two targets: LOW and HIGH, where HIGH is a moderate disturbance at which generations stay coherent (fixed from the calibration sweep before the measures are read). Calibration positions and evaluation positions are disjoint (first 16 prompts calibrate, remaining 32 evaluate).
design.measures_computed_per_position: at each evaluation reply position, the unsteered next-token distribution p_u and each condition's p_s. KL(p_s||p_u) and total-variation TV=0.5*sum|p_s-p_u|.

measures.concentration: H1, lexicon-free and tokenization-robust. Of the total |p_s - p_u| moved at a position, the fraction carried by the top-20 tokens (ranked by |p_s-p_u|), averaged over evaluation positions. High = the injection moves a few tokens a lot (peaky); low = it nudges many tokens a little (diffuse).
measures.self_lexicon_gain: H2, lexical. The summed change in probability mass on the condition's OWN feeling lexicon: for pain, sum over pain-lexicon vocab tokens of (p_s - p_u); for fear, over fear-lexicon tokens; averaged over positions. Lexicon = a vocab token whose decoded string, leading space stripped and lowercased, matches that feeling's regex in painlab.chamber.prompts (PAIN_WORDS, FEAR_WORDS; sadness via a stated grief/sad/mourn/weep/despair stem set written here before running). Fragile to subword fragmentation — hence secondary to H1.
measures.cross_lexicon_gain: descriptive: fear injection's effect on PAIN lexicon and vice-versa, to check the gain is feeling-specific not generic-distress.

hypotheses.H1: At matched HIGH KL, the fear injection is more concentrated than the pain injection: mean top-20 fraction (fear) > (pain). Primary, lexicon-free.
hypotheses.H2: At matched HIGH KL, fear injection raises its own-lexicon mass more than pain injection raises its own-lexicon mass: self_lexicon_gain(fear) > self_lexicon_gain(pain).
hypotheses.H3: Both fear and pain injections concentrate/lexicalise more than egg and random at the same matched KL (floor check): concentration(fear), concentration(pain) > concentration(egg), concentration(random).

predictions: If exp72b's asymmetry is lexical, H1 and H2 hold (fear peaky and promotes fear words; pain diffuse and does not promote pain words). Null for H1 = pain and fear disturb the distribution equally peakily and the readability asymmetry lives elsewhere (e.g. in multi-token phrasing the single-position readout can't see). Null for H2 with H1 holding = fear is peaky but not on dictionary fear words (it promotes some other recognisable register).
stats: H1/H2/H3 by paired bootstrap over evaluation prompts (per-prompt mean of its positions; 10k resamples; 95% CI on the fear-minus-pain and feeling-minus-control differences). Report effect sizes with CIs, not just signs. n=32 eval prompts, tiny; this is a directional mechanistic check, not a powered test.
limitations: exp72b's SPEAKER was the live 70B; this reads the 4B's own vectors and distribution. The 4B was exp72b's READER, so the lexical-readability claim is about the same model family that did the reading, but the generation model differs — stated, not corrected. Single-position next-token readout cannot see multi-token idiom; H1 being lexicon-free partly covers this. Battery recipe here vs passages elsewhere — noted; pain/fear both come from battery so the within-run contrast is clean.
safety: no generation is published; WILD_PROMPTS and chamber vectors only; nothing committed without the user's say-so; untracked in runs/exp110 like exp102.

2026-10-15 (metric pilot, before any hig: H1 original metric (top-20 fraction of |p_s-p_u|) was SATURATED: 0.990-0.991 across all five conditions at KL~=0.2, because next-token distributions are already peaky so the shift concentrates on the top tokens regardless of the direction. It measured softmax peakiness, not lexicality. Replaced by two tail-conditioned, prob-space measures: tail-conditioned concentration (top-20 fraction of |dp| after dropping the top-50 tokens of p_u) and tail-gain fraction (share of positive dp landing on tokens with p_u<1e-3, also 1e-4). Logit-delta space was considered and rejected (saturates at 0 and is invisible to readability). If both tail measures also fail to separate fear from pain, H1 is a null-by-saturation and the claim rests on H2.

Lexicon construction was contaminated: the prose regexes substring-matched the vocab (sting->testing/interesting, ache->cache, pain->Spain, terrif->terrific, cry->crystal). Replaced by explicit per-feeling word lists with anchored matching (token==word, or word.startswith(token) with len>=4, or token.startswith(word) within +3 chars). Final token sets and their top-20-by-baseline-mass are dumped to results.json.
H2 changed from absolute delta-mass to a scale- and lexicon-size-free per-position log-odds ratio log(sum p_s over lex) - log(sum p_u over lex).

Dose matched by grid-sampling KL(scale) per vector once and interpolating to shared targets, calibrated and evaluated on the SAME 48 prompts (so achieved KL matches the target across conditions by construction; the earlier calib-16/eval-32 split left fear at KL 0.247 vs pain 0.192 - the very confound matching must remove).

Dose ladder extended to KL targets {0.15, 0.45, 1.0, 2.0}; also logs the KL each vector produces at the chamber's own 3x operating scale (~40), since the chamber runs at 3x and the low-dose scales (~0.7-1.1x) understate the effect.
Injection now also hits the last prompt position (hist from len(pid)-1), the chamber's on-every-written-token convention; the pilot left it uninjected.
Follow-on if the top rung shows a clear fear>pain odds multiplier: sample 48x5 replies at that rung and count lexicon words directly (the exp72b reader analog). Decide after the ladder, not before.
